3) Around line 308 the authors describe that the weak fold difference in K9me3 levels between the truncated and full-length copies is likely a sever underestimation because non-unique mappings are distributed evenly amongst copies. Why did the authors not look at unique mappers?

4) In Figure 7B-C it is perplexing that the H3K9me3 enrichment in the last 1kb of internal sequence of TEs is higher in the full-length, while in the first 1kb internal sequence it is higher in the truncated copies. How do the authors explain this difference?

5) References remain insufficient and often wrong or at least not referring to the primary/first discovery. It is very apparent that the authors have not obtained a broad knowledge of the piRNA field and/or have done a sloppy job with the references even after this was raised in the first round of review. Here are some examples:

– Line 42: While I am not sure why the authors bring phase separation into this story, if they do, they should also be aware of counter-arguments to HP1 inducing phase separation (Erdel et al., 2020. PMID: 32101700).

– Line 51-53: The authors refer to results in flies and mice but only reference a single fly paper. Shortly after (line 57), they cite 3 papers (not correctly formatted) for Piwi causing H3K9 methylation, yet one of them, Derricarrere et al., only showed that Piwi cleavage activity is needed and did not provide any analysis of its role in H3K9 methylation, while some relevant papers are missing.

– Line 59-61: The authors say that the piRNA-Piwi complex recruits heterochromatin factors, including histone methyltransferases for H3K9me3 deposition. The papers cited refer to Piwi inducing H3K9me3, without either of them showing recruitment of the HMT. On the other hand, they miss citing the paper that comes closest to showing recruitment mechanism of the HMT. In addition, they cite one of two papers describing Panx (why not the paper by Brennecke?) and one on the SFINX complex (this time only the Brennecke paper out of 4 parallel papers), the first a factor of unknown function and the 2nd an RNA binding complex. This seems like a random choice of factors (excluding Arx, the RDC complex, etc.) and a random choice of references for those.

6) Figures and figure legends:

– Figure legend 5: panel "C" is missing.

– Color scheme in Figure 4H is missing?

– Figure 7B-D it would help if the panels would indicate what the difference is so one does not have to look in the figure legend.

– For suppl. figure 5 and 7Y axis label is missing. Are these different stages?

– For suppl. figure 11 the colors are not indicated (for the different stages, so one hast to look at the main figures to know what stage is which color). Also, the "position of called peaks" indicated at the top of panels would need to be mentioned in the figure legends in all figures.

Just a suggestion: While the figures are very nice in color (and consistent throughout the manuscript), the color choices are making it essentially impossible to look at the data on a black and white printout. While this is by itself not a huge issue, I generally prefer plots that do not depend on color printouts. E.g., in Figure 3E-F the two colors look identical in BandW and, accordingly, it is impossible to determine what the lower and upper half of the chromosome arm markings are in 3F. If the colors are left the same, it would help to better describe this in the figure legends. Numerous other examples of colors being hard to evaluate in BandW are found, that I do not list.

Reviewer #4 (Recommendations for the authors):

Summary:

Wei et al., determined genome-wide repressive histone H3 lysine K9 trimethylation (H3K9me3) marks during precisely timed developmental stages in Drosophila miranda embryos. Heterochromatin formation by H3K9me3 was profiled starting 3.5 hours post fertilization (9 cell divisions, "stage 3") up to gastrulation (14 cell divisions, "stage 7"). While a proportion of stage 3 were transient, early stage 4 H3K9me3 peaks seem to nucleate and correlate very well with repressive chromatin spreading in later stages.

The authors profile RNA expression at several stages as well as maternally deposited small RNAs right after fertilization ("stage 1"). The RNA expression data confirms silencing of loci that nucleate heterochromatin formation at stage 4. Wei et al. find abundant PIWI-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) that target transposon sequences and examine their potential to guide H3K9me3 deposition as previously observed in Drosphila melanogaster and other organisms. Transposons that have repressive H3K9me3 marks at stage 3 are piRNA targets, suggesting maternally deposited piRNAs may guide this early heterochromatin induction. However, piRNA target sites do not correlate with H3K9me3 positions at these loci, making the link between stage 1 piRNAs and transcriptional silencing at stage 3 rather speculative.

The detailed H3K9me3 data in D. miranda reveals interesting patterns of heterochromatin establishment over transposable elements (TEs). Several LTR-retrotransposons exhibit nucleation at their 5'-end, while other non-LTR elements show early enrichment at their 3'-ends. This is similar and interesting when compared to 5'-nucleation patterns of H3K9me3 during epigenetic reprogramming at TEs in mammals.

1) The H3K9me3 patterns along TEs are intriguing and very interesting. The authors may want to group and present TEs by class, at least discuss them by class in the text. This may explain "discrepancies" between transposon families. It seems LTR-retroelements show 5'-nucleation while non-LTR elements have a 3'-bias? The findings could be further elevated by discussing patterns in other organisms, perhaps data in D. melanogaster is available? In mouse and primates, 5'-nucleation has been observed by: Rebollo, 2011 Plos Genetics; Wolf, 2015 Genes Dev; Walter, 2016 eLife; Imbeault, 2017 Nature; Wolf, 2020 eLife.

In mouse and human, this nucleation is often (but perhaps not always) guided by ZFP which the authors point out are not conserved in flies. Given the similar patterns, this may still point to a highly conserved targeting mechanism for H3K9me3.

H3K9me3 induction at several LTR-retroelements in mouse have been shown to initiate at their highly conserved tRNA primer binding site and spread from there (Rebollo, 2011 Plos Genetics; Wolf, 2015 Genes Dev). It would be helpful if the authors state more precisely what they defined as a "5'-truncation". How many nucleotides were missing in these copies? Only 5'-LTRs or perhaps additional nucleotides from the 5'-UTR?

2) The correlation between piRNAs and H3K9me3 peaks seems marginal if at all. The last sentence of the abstract, while most likely true, seems a gross over-interpretation of the results. While I can well imagine how small RNA at one stage guide H3K9me3 at a later stage, the absence of correlation with H3K9me3 peaks make this scenario a long stretch. Therefore, the reasoning in the manuscript becomes pretty confusing. That maternally deposited piRNAs may be instrumental in suppressing this group of TEs is interesting and well possible but hard to conclude from the presented data.

On the piRNA data presentation: I don't see the value in showing correlation lines and r-values in figures 6D, E, F, 4H when there is no correlation visible. 3H, S9 (x-axis = kb from peak?) make the reader wonder how piRNA distribution look like further (than 2kb) away from the peak of H3K9me3. Is there any accumulation around peaks? Perhaps piRNA accumulation and distribution could be better grasped in browser shots like S5 and S7 with an additional piRNA track?

What is the y-axis unit in Figure 5D, G, J? For small RNAs, it is common to calculate normalized read counts in RPM (reads per total mio mapped). However, 5000RPM would be a lot?! (10,000RPM = 1% of the library) Readers need to be able to judge expression strength and depth.

Figure 6 is confusing: while it looks like lots of piRNAs map to stage 3 TEs in panel A and B, panel D (and E) shows no correlation whatsoever. Maybe it could be pointed out more clearly that A+B are about distinct TEs, while D+E are about H3K9me3 position within an element? I took the conclusion that piRNAs "mark" stage 3 high copy number TEs from panel F.

3) Much of the RNA expression data is plotted like one would plot chromatin peaks and a bit odd presentation of "no expression". In Figure S6 and 3G (upper third coordinates) there are a couple of loci that are expressed throughout stages. What are they? Are they independent of H3K9me3 and are they a specific transposon family? Genic? The obtained RNAseq data should be more accessible, which portions of the genome are expressed at the stages sampled? Perhaps some pie charts or supplemental tables of where in the genome reads map to at which stage could provide an overview of what the RNAseq actually revealed other than negative correlation with H3K9me3 at select loci.

4) The piRNA references are outdated and additional references would make the authors point only stronger.

– Line 53 and 256 (and others): There are excellent reviews on transcriptional silencing through the piRNA pathway that are much more recent than 2009, e.g. Ninova, 2019 Dev; Olovnikov, 2012 Curr Opin Genet Dev; Ozata, 2019 Nature Rev Genetics

– Line 53: Brennecke et al., 2007 was a foundational paper to characterize piRNA cluster and PIWI-mediated post-transcriptional silencing of TEs in Drosophila but does not show transcriptional silencing. Several other studies later did which would be more accurate to cite here, if the authors don't want to cite a review. E.g.:

Drosophila: Sienski et al., 2012 Cell (cited elsewhere); Le Thomas et al., 2013 Genes Dev (cited elsewhere); Huang et al., 2013 Dev Cell; Mammals: Watanabe 2011 Science; Aravin 2008 Mol Cell; Pezic, 2014 Genes Dev; C. elegans: Gu et al., 2012 Nature Genetics

– Line 345: If the point is metazoan, gametogenesis and preimplantation… add such references to Wang et al., 2018. E.g. Tang et al., 2016 Nat Rev Genet; Laue et al., 2019 Nature Comm (zebrafish); Ishiuchi et al., 2021 NSMB; Saitou et al., 2012 Dev (review)

claims.claim: Diminished H3K9me3 enrichment is not observed from 3' truncated TRAM copies where the 5' LTR remains intact.
claims.source: Notably, diminished H3K9me3 enrichment is not observed from 3' truncated TRAM copies (n = 51, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) where the 5' LTR remains intact (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 2); in fact, 3' truncated TRAM copies have elevated enrichment compared to full-length copies as they, by necessity, contain proportionally more of the highly enriched 5' sequences (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the comparison of 3' truncated and full-length TRAM copies shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: 5' truncated insertions of TRAM tend to be more accessible based on ATAC-seq enrichment.
claims.source: Further supporting the functional importance of the promoter adjacent nucleating sites for heterochromatin establishment, we find that 5' truncated insertions of TRAM tend to be more accessible based on ATAC-seq enrichment; albeit, the differences are either marginally significant or insignificant (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 7D.

results.result: H3K9me3-dependent heterochromatin establishment begins at or before early stage 4 (nuclear cycle 10/11) in D. miranda embryos, earlier than previously observed by cytology. The number of H3K9me3 peaks increases sharply from stage 3 (n=2202) to early stage 4 (n=51,202), with enrichment observed around pericentric regions and subsequent increases through stage 7.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C52-C54, and C60 are well-supported by ChIP-seq data showing clear H3K9me3 enrichment at early stage 4 and peak calling analysis (Figure 2A-B). The interpretation that heterochromatin establishment starts at or before stage 4 is consistent with the observed enrichment patterns. The data directly contradict prior cytological observations (C38-C39) that placed heterochromatin appearance at late stage 4/cell cycle 13, demonstrating the higher sensitivity of ChIP-seq.

results.result: H3K9me3 nucleation sites appear as early as stage 3 over transposable elements and progressively broaden across development, consistent with spreading to neighboring nucleosomes. Nearly 60% of stage 7 peaks already show enrichment at early stage 4, and an additional 27% show enrichment at stage 3. Peak sizes broaden and become less sharp as development progresses.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C55-C59, and C65 are strongly supported by ChIP-seq data showing early nucleation and progressive broadening (Figures 2C-E, 3B-C). The interpretation of spreading to neighboring nucleosomes is reasonable given the observed broadening pattern, though direct evidence of nucleosome-by-nucleosome spreading is not provided. The quantitative data on peak overlap across stages (C58-C59) is clearly presented in Figure 2E.

results.result: Stage 3 peaks (n=997 after filtering) show sharp and narrow enrichment (median width 125 bp) around their center, consistent with single nucleosomes, and differ strikingly from peaks at later stages. Control ChIP experiments against H3, H3K4me3, and H4K16ac were used to filter out 1205 non-specific peaks.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C64 and C66 are well-supported by data in Figures 2B-C and 3A. The control experiments (C63) strengthen confidence in the specificity of stage 3 peaks. The interpretation that 125 bp peaks represent single nucleosomes (C66) is reasonable given the known ~147 bp DNA wrapping around nucleosomes, though the claim acknowledges this is a suggestion rather than definitive proof.

results.result: Early nucleation sites are restricted to specific regions of a small number of recently active retrotransposon families, often appearing over promoter and 5' regions of LTR retrotransposons (e.g., TRAM at 0-300 bp). Only 35 of 235 TE entries (14.8%) overlap with stage 3 peaks, while 189 (80.3%) overlap with early stage 4 peaks. Stage 3 peaks are scattered across the genome rather than concentrated in pericentric regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C9, C67-C69, C73-C74, C103-C105, C107-C110, and C113 are strongly supported by detailed analysis of H3K9me3 enrichment patterns on specific TEs (Figures 5A-G, 3E-F). The data clearly show restricted nucleation at specific TE positions at stage 3 followed by broader enrichment at stage 4. The genomic distribution analysis (Figure 3F) confirms the unexpected scattered distribution of stage 3 peaks.

results.result: 25.6% (n=256) of stage 3 peaks appear to become depleted of H3K9me3 enrichment over time (temporary peaks). These temporary peaks predominantly overlap microsatellites (71.4%) rather than TEs (3.1%) and are found outside pericentromeric regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 and C75 are supported by data in Figures 3B, D-F, but the authors themselves note uncertainty about whether these represent failed nucleation sites or residual phantom peaks after filtering (C70). The distinct genomic features of temporary peaks (microsatellite enrichment, non-pericentric location) suggest they may be biologically distinct, but without functional validation or additional controls, the interpretation remains uncertain.

results.result: Early nucleating TEs are strongly associated with abundant maternal piRNAs and show early zygotic transcription. Persistent stage 3 peaks have significantly higher piRNA mapping (median RPM=15.55) compared to the rest of the genome (1.48) and pericentromeric regions without peaks (10.36), while temporary stage 3 peaks have almost no piRNA mapping (median RPM=0). Similar patterns are observed for stage 4 peaks.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11, C76-C81, C98-C101, and C114-C116 are well-supported by piRNA-seq and RNA-seq data (Figures 3G, 4H, 6A-D). Statistical testing with Wilcoxon rank sum tests shows significant differences (p<2.2e-16). The association between piRNA abundance and early nucleation is clear, though the mechanistic interpretation (C80, C116) is inferential. The RNA-seq data showing early zygotic transcription (C11) is consistent with co-transcriptional silencing models.

results.result: The results support a model of piRNA-associated co-transcriptional silencing but also suggest additional mechanisms for site-restricted H3K9me3 nucleation. Regions with abundant piRNA mapping on TEs do not necessarily correspond to positions of stage 3 peaks, and the amount of piRNA mapping shows little-to-no correlation with H3K9me3 enrichment at any given position along TEs.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13 and C123-C126 are supported by the lack of spatial correlation between piRNA mapping and H3K9me3 enrichment positions (Figures 5D, G, J; 6E; Figure 6—supplement 1). While piRNA abundance at the TE level correlates with early nucleation, the positional mismatch argues against a simple targeting model and supports the need for additional mechanisms. This is a reasonable interpretation of the data, though the specific alternative mechanisms remain speculative.

results.result: The number of H3K9me3 peaks increases drastically from ~1000 at stage 3 to 52,607 at early stage 4. Early stage 4 peaks can be divided into 16,630 'old' peaks (showing enrichment at stage 3) and 35,977 'new' peaks (no prior enrichment). Old peaks are significantly wider (847 bp vs 378 bp) and show secondary peaks indicating spreading to adjacent nucleosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C93 are well-supported by peak calling analysis and characterization (Figures 4A-D, Figure 4—supplements 1-2). The statistical comparison of peak widths (C88) includes appropriate testing (Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<2.2e-16). The observation of secondary peaks around old peaks (C89) and the interpretation of spreading is reasonable, though the mechanism is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: Both old and new early stage 4 peaks show decreasing chromatin accessibility over development as measured by ATAC-seq, with old peaks being significantly less accessible across all stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 are supported by ATAC-seq data (Figure 4E). The inverse relationship between H3K9me3 enrichment and chromatin accessibility is expected and validates the functional consequence of heterochromatin formation. The statistical significance of differences between old and new peaks is stated but specific p-values are not provided in the claim text.

results.result: Most stage 4 peaks (84.2%) overlap with annotated TEs, and 82.6% are concentrated at the pericentromere and repeat-rich Y chromosome.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C97 are supported by overlap analysis (Figures 4F-G). This represents the expected localization of heterochromatin to repetitive sequences and validates the biological relevance of the identified peaks.

results.result: Many windows with stage 4 peaks have no piRNAs mapping, and many windows without peaks have high piRNAs mapping, suggesting additional signals beyond piRNAs are at play.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 is supported by the distribution shown in Figure 4H. This observation reinforces the conclusion that piRNA abundance alone does not fully explain H3K9me3 targeting patterns, supporting the need for additional mechanisms (C13, C126).

results.result: Three TE variants (CR1-1, LOA-3, and Gypsy18) have the most early stage 4 peaks but few stage 3 peaks, suggesting some TEs nucleate heterochromatin earlier than others.
results.evaluation: Claim C106 is supported by data in Figure 5A showing differential timing of nucleation across TE families. This observation is important for understanding the heterogeneity in heterochromatin establishment.

results.result: The 5' region of TRAM continues to increase in H3K9me3 over development. Nearly all 748 TRAM copies show elevated H3K9me3 enrichment at their 5' region even though only 27 peaks were called there, indicating peak calling substantially underestimates nucleation sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C112 are supported by analysis of TRAM insertions (Figure 5E, G). The observation that peak calling is conservative (C112) is important for interpreting the quantitative results and suggests the actual number of nucleation sites is higher than reported peak counts.

results.result: piRNA abundance is much more strongly and significantly correlated with H3K9me3 enrichment of TEs at later developmental stages, which could indicate piRNAs facilitate spreading and maturation of H3K9me3-dependent silencing after early nucleation.
results.evaluation: Claim C117 is supported by correlation analysis (Figure 6B). The interpretation that piRNAs facilitate spreading is speculative but reasonable given the data. The correlation strengthening over time is clearly shown, though the mechanistic interpretation requires further validation.

results.result: TEs with stage 3 peaks are significantly lower in transcript abundance across all stages but show the highest and earliest increase in transcript abundance. Stage 3 nucleating TEs show a 1.41-fold increase in RNA abundance from stage 2 to stage 4, while most TEs remain unchanged (0.97-fold). TEs with stage 4 peaks show evidence of zygotic transcription between stages 4 and 5.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C122 are supported by RNA-seq analysis (Figure 6C-D). The data show early nucleating TEs are among the first to be zygotically transcribed, consistent with co-transcriptional silencing models. The fold-change values are specific and appear to be derived from the data, though the statistical significance of the 1.41-fold change is not explicitly stated.

results.result: The 5' LTR of TRAM is highly enriched for H3K9me3. 5' truncated TRAM copies lacking the 5' LTR are significantly less enriched for H3K9me3 (1.36-fold difference at stage 7) and tend to be more accessible by ATAC-seq. 3' truncated copies with intact 5' LTR show no diminished enrichment.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C131 are supported by comparison of full-length and truncated TRAM insertions (Figure 7A-D). This provides functional evidence for the importance of 5' nucleation sites. However, the authors note the 1.36-fold difference is likely an underestimate due to cross-mapping between copies. The ATAC-seq differences are marginally significant or insignificant (C131), which weakens but does not invalidate the overall conclusion.

results.result: The amount of piRNA mapping to TEs is significantly anti-correlated with maternally deposited transcript abundance (r=-0.54, p<2.2e-16). TEs with stage 3 nucleation are significantly overrepresented with lowly expressing TEs (p=1.582e-08) and remain lowly expressed as zygotic transcription increases, indicating early nucleating TEs are among the most repressed.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C135 are supported by correlation and expression analysis (Figure 6C, F). The statistical tests are appropriate and significant. The interpretation that early nucleating TEs are among the most repressed (C135) is reasonable given the data, though it is somewhat inferential.

results.result: Early nucleating TEs are significantly more abundant in both male and female D. miranda genomes. The neo-Y has on average 1.79-fold more early nucleating TEs than the rest of the genome, indicating these TEs have been recently active in the D. miranda lineage.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C138 are supported by copy number analysis (Figure 8A-B). The enrichment on the neo-Y, which formed 1.5 million years ago, provides strong evidence for recent activity. This connects the molecular findings to evolutionary dynamics and explains why these TEs are subject to robust silencing.

results.result: H3K9me3 and H3K9me2 enrichment profiles are very similar and highly correlated.
results.evaluation: Claim C139 is supported by comparison of H3K9me3 and H3K9me2 ChIP-seq from the same embryos (Figure 1—supplement 1). This validates the use of H3K9me3 as a marker for heterochromatin in this system.

results.result: Background claims about heterochromatin function, H3K9me3 biology, piRNA pathways, and D. miranda genome characteristics based on established knowledge and cited literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C14-C42, and C140 represent established knowledge from the literature and are appropriately cited. These provide necessary context for interpreting the novel findings. The citations appear appropriate, though detailed verification of each cited claim is beyond the scope of this evaluation.

results.result: The D. miranda genome assembly has near end-to-end assemblies including ~30 Mb of pericentromeric heterochromatin and >100 Mb of the neo-Y chromosome assembled into two massive contigs (53.8 and 37.2 Mb). The genome has few simple satellites, allowing ChIP-seq mapping of heterochromatic regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C51 describe the D. miranda genome assembly and are supported by citations to prior work (Mahajan et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2018, 2020) and Figure 1C-D. The quality of the genome assembly is crucial for the validity of the ChIP-seq mapping, and these claims establish that D. miranda is an appropriate system for this study.
